advisory.summary: A Bugsink issue-event page loaded the event by id without scoping it to the issue in the URL, so a member of one project read another project's event data through an issue they could access.
note: GHSA-vx2f-6m6h-9frf. The issue_event_stacktrace/_details/_breadcrumbs
views are only @issue_membership_required: they check membership of the
URL's ISSUE, then _get_event did Event.objects.get(pk=event_pk) on the
caller-supplied event id ALONE. So a user who is a member of their own
project names their own issue and another project's event id and reads
that event -- exception type and value, rendered on the stacktrace page.
2.2.0 matches Event.objects.get(issue=issue, pk=event_pk); when it does
not match it renders an 'event not in this issue' page, still HTTP 200.
So the status is 200 on BOTH builds and only the planted marker (the
exception value) distinguishes them -- a status oracle is blind to the
fix, like the lubelogger pair. The owner reading its own event in the
control is the live positive: its 200+marker on 2.2.0 proves the marker
is reachable, so the attacker's marker-free 200 there is the fix.
Confirmed from source inside both images: 2.1.3 issues/views.py has
Event.objects.get(pk=event_pk); 2.2.0 has Event.objects.get(issue=issue,
pk=event_pk). Image version labels read 2.1.3 and 2.2.0.
Bugsink issue-event pages authenticate with a Django session cookie, so
each identity is a static Cookie header, filled from a session minted
through the app's own ORM.
Measured by hand on both tags before this was written: the attacker
reads the owner's event (200 + marker) on 2.1.3 and gets a marker-free
200 on 2.2.0; its session is valid on 2.2.0 (it reads its own event 200),
so the exclusion is the fix, not a refused credential; the owner is 403
on the attacker's issue on both tags.
The second check is the direct route: the attacker names the OWNER's
issue and event, and is refused 403 without the marker on both tags,
while the owner reads the same page 200 with the marker (measured on
2.1.3 and 2.2.0 on 2026-09-27; it had been inferred by symmetry from the
owner's 403 on the attacker's issue). So the leak needs the unscoped
event lookup, not a missing membership check on the issue. A fabricated
or absent session is 302 to /accounts/login/ on both, so a 403 here is
an authorization refusal of a live session, not a dead credential.
vulnerable_failing_checks names the first check alone, so every run
holds the 2.1.3 half too: a finding from the direct route on 2.1.3
fails the pair (scripts/patched_pairs.py, evaluate).

checks.name: A project member must not read another project's event through an issue of its own
A member of another project must not read the owner's event through the owner's own issue
